title: CIS Controls and Benchmarks
subtitle: All 153 Safeguards, the Benchmarks and the CIS toolset
source: Based on the CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1, the CIS Controls Assessment Specification, CIS Benchmarks documentation and the CIS Community Defense Model v2.0. Safeguard requirements are paraphrased
description: CIS from A to Z: the ecosystem, all 18 Controls and 153 Safeguards with Implementation Groups, practice guidance and examples, how CIS Benchmarks are built and read, how to implement them, the CIS tools, and how to run and report a CIS programme.

chapters.title: CIS and its ecosystem
chapters.summary: Who CIS is, the family of CIS resources, and how Controls and Benchmarks fit together.

blocks.text: The **Center for Internet Security (CIS)** is a US-based non-profit founded in 2000. Its stated mission is to make the connected world a safer place by developing, validating and promoting best-practice security guidance. CIS content is built by volunteer communities of practitioners, vendors, government and academia, and is used by organisations worldwide.
For this book, two CIS products matter most:

items: **CIS Critical Security Controls (CIS Controls):** a prioritised set of 18 Controls and 153 Safeguards describing what an organisation should do to defend against the most common attacks.
**CIS Benchmarks:** consensus-based secure configuration guides for specific technologies, such as Windows 11, Ubuntu, AWS or Microsoft 365. They describe exactly how to configure a system securely.

blocks.title: Why CIS is popular
blocks.text: CIS content is free to download for internal use, vendor-neutral, practical and prioritised. Smaller organisations like that it starts with a short list (IG1); auditors and insurers like that it is specific and testable.

sections.title: How Controls and Benchmarks fit together

blocks.text: The simplest way to hold the whole CIS ecosystem in your head is **what, how, pre-built and proof**:

rows: What should our security programme do, and in what order?
Exactly which settings make this operating system, database or cloud account secure?
Can we start from an already-hardened image or apply settings in bulk?
How far are we from the target, and is it improving?
Is this level of effort reasonable for our risk, and does it defend against real attacks?

blocks.text: The explicit link is Safeguard **4.1 Establish and Maintain a Secure Configuration Process**. The Controls say you must have secure configurations; the Benchmarks are the most widely used way to define them. Every Benchmark recommendation is also mapped back to the Safeguards it supports.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A hospital adopts IG1. For Safeguard 4.1 it chooses the CIS Microsoft Windows 11 Enterprise Benchmark (Level 1) for clinical workstations, applies it with a Build Kit GPO, and measures compliance monthly with CIS-CAT. Progress on the Safeguards is tracked in CSAT.

sections.title: CIS compared with NIST CSF and ISO 27001

US federal systems, detailed control design

blocks.title: They work together
blocks.text: A common pattern: NIST CSF 2.0 as the outcome framework and board reporting language, CIS Controls as the implementation checklist, CIS Benchmarks for technical settings, and ISO/IEC 27001 when certification is required.

sections.title: Licensing: what you may do with CIS content

blocks.text: CIS content is free to **use** inside your organisation, but it is not public domain. The CIS Controls document is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence, and Benchmark PDFs are free for non-commercial use.

items: **Fine without a licence:** downloading the Controls and Benchmarks to secure your own organisation, training your staff, referencing them in policies.

**Needs checking:** embedding CIS content in a commercial product (for example an assessment or GRC tool), reselling it, or using member-only formats and tools. CIS offers SecureSuite memberships and product vendor agreements for these cases.
**Consultants:** check the current terms of use before putting CIS content into paid client deliverables or tools.

blocks.title: Check before you build
blocks.text: If you build software that ships the CIS Safeguard text or Benchmark recommendations, get the licence position confirmed with CIS first. The terms can change, and "it's free to download" is not the same as "it's free to redistribute".

chapters.title: CIS Controls fundamentals
chapters.summary: History, design principles, structure, the 18 Controls at a glance, and how to read a Safeguard.

rows: Origin as a US government and industry effort to list the most important defensive actions against real attacks (early names included the Consensus Audit Guidelines and the SANS Top 20)
CIS becomes the steward of the Controls
Version 7: 20 Controls grouped as Basic, Foundational and Organizational
Version 7.1 introduces Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2, IG3)

Version 8: consolidated to 18 Controls; sub-controls renamed Safeguards (153 in total); organised by activity rather than by who manages a device; cloud, mobile and remote work reflected; new Control 15 Service Provider Management

Version 8.1: adds the Govern security function, aligns security functions with NIST CSF 2.0, adds Documentation as an asset class, expands the glossary and clarifies Safeguard wording. Implementation Groups unchanged
Updated v8.1 guide with minor corrections

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: v8 and v8.1 both have **18 Controls and 153 Safeguards**. v8.1 changed classifications and wording, not the number of Safeguards or the IG assignments. CIS has said it is working on ideas for Version 9; check the CIS website for its status.
CIS describes the Controls as guided by five design principles:

rows: Safeguards are chosen and prioritised based on data about how real attacks happen
Help defenders identify the most critical things to do first, and avoid the temptation to solve every problem
Recommendations are specific and practical to implement
Safeguards are written so their implementation can be measured, with thresholds where possible (e.g. 45 days, 90 days)
The Controls map to other frameworks, regulations and standards so that one effort serves many requirements

blocks.title: The "Fog of More"
blocks.text: CIS created the Controls to cut through what it calls the Fog of More: too many tools, frameworks and opinions. The Controls say: start with these, in this order.

sections.title: Structure: Controls, Safeguards, asset classes and functions

blocks.text: Each **Control** is a family of related activities with an overview and a statement of why it matters. Each Control contains **Safeguards**: specific, measurable actions. Every Safeguard carries four attributes:

rows: Devices, Software, Data, Users, Network, Documentation
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Aligns with the NIST CSF 2.0 functions
Priority: which organisations should implement it

blocks.text: In CIS terms: assets with the potential to store or process data, including end-user devices, network devices, non-computing/IoT devices and servers, in virtual, cloud and physical environments.
Added in v8.1 for plans, policies, processes and procedures, which many Safeguards require you to establish and maintain.

blocks.title: About the labels in this book
blocks.text: Each Safeguard card in this book shows its number, lowest Implementation Group and security function. Titles and IGs match the CIS Controls. Security functions follow CIS's published Assessment Specification, updated for v8.1's Govern function on policy and process Safeguards. If an audit depends on the exact v8.1 classification, check the official CIS Controls v8.1 spreadsheet.

rows: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
Inventory and Control of Software Assets
Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

blocks.title: Notice the pattern
blocks.text: The first Controls build the foundation (know your assets, data and configurations). Controls 13, 16 and 18 have no IG1 Safeguards at all because they need specialised tools or skills.
Safeguards are short, but the wording is precise:

items: **"Establish and maintain"** means a documented, approved artefact (policy, process, inventory) that is reviewed on a schedule, usually annually "or when significant enterprise changes occur".
**Frequencies are minimums.** "Monthly, or more frequently" means monthly is the floor.
**"Where supported"** means apply it wherever the technology allows, and document where it doesn't.
**Thresholds are specific:** 15-minute screen lock, 45 days for dormant accounts, 90 days of log retention, quarterly restore tests.
**Dependencies matter:** most Safeguards assume inventories from Controls 1, 2, 3 and 5 exist. The Assessment Specification lists the dependencies for each Safeguard.

blocks.title: Reading a card
blocks.text: **6.5 | IG1 | Protect** means Safeguard 6.5 (Require MFA for Administrative Access), included from IG1 upwards, and part of the Protect function.

chapters.title: Implementation Groups
chapters.summary: IG1, IG2 and IG3: who they are for, how many Safeguards each has, and how to choose.

blocks.text: Implementation Groups (IGs) are CIS's built-in prioritisation. Each IG is a self-assessed category based on an organisation's resources, risk and the sensitivity of its data. IGs are **cumulative**: IG2 includes all of IG1, and IG3 includes all of IG1 and IG2.

rows: Small to medium organisation with limited IT and security expertise; mostly protects employee and financial data. Needs Safeguards that work with commercial off-the-shelf tools and little specialist knowledge. Goal: stop general, untargeted attacks.

Has staff responsible for managing and protecting IT; several departments with different risk profiles; stores sensitive client or enterprise data; could lose public confidence after a breach. Some Safeguards need enterprise-grade technology and specialist skills.

Employs security specialists (risk, penetration testing, application security); holds sensitive data subject to regulatory oversight; a successful attack could cause significant harm to the public. Must withstand targeted attacks from sophisticated adversaries and reduce the impact of zero-days.

blocks.title: Remember the numbers
blocks.text: **56 / 130 / 153.** IG1 = 56 Safeguards. IG2 adds 74 (130 in total). IG3 adds 23 (all 153).
CIS calls IG1 **essential cyber hygiene**: the minimum standard of information security that every organisation, of any size, should meet. It covers:

items: Knowing your hardware, software, data and accounts (1.1, 2.1, 3.2, 5.1).
Secure configuration, firewalls and screen locking (4.1-4.7).
MFA for external apps, remote access and admins (6.3-6.5).
Automated OS and application patching (7.3, 7.4).
Collecting logs and keeping enough storage (8.2, 8.3).
Anti-malware, DNS filtering and supported browsers (9.1, 9.2, 10.1-10.3).
Automated, protected and isolated backups (11.1-11.4).
Keeping network infrastructure supported and up to date (12.1) and knowing your service providers (15.1).
Security awareness training (14.1-14.8).
Basic incident response: who's in charge, who to call, how staff report (17.1-17.3).

blocks.title: Why IG1 is a strong default
blocks.text: IG1 is short enough for a small IT team to complete in months, yet CIS's own analysis shows it defends against most techniques used in common attacks. For many mid-market clients, "IG1 fully implemented and evidenced" is a better goal than "IG3 partially implemented".

rows: Customer personal data, payment data, health data, IP
Sector regulators, data protection authorities, PCI DSS, critical infrastructure rules
Small generalist IT team or outsourced
Dedicated IT operations and security teams
Targeted attacks, nation-state interest, high-value transactions
Impact of an outage or breach

blocks.text: You don't have to apply one IG everywhere. A common approach is to implement IG1 organisation-wide first, then IG2 across the enterprise, and apply selected IG3 Safeguards to the most critical systems (the "crown jewels").

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A 300-person logistics company with no dedicated security team targets IG1 in year one. Its customer portal and payment integration then receive selected IG2 Safeguards (3.10, 3.11, 7.5-7.7, 8.5, 8.9-8.11) because they process customer and card data.

The **CIS Community Defense Model (CDM) v2.0** (2021) mapped the Safeguards against MITRE ATT&CK techniques used in the five most prevalent attack types: malware, ransomware, web application hacking, insider privilege and misuse, and targeted intrusions. CIS's published findings:

rows: ATT&CK (sub-)techniques used in the top five attack types
All ATT&CK (sub-)techniques, regardless of attack type

blocks.text: CDM v2.0 also found Safeguard **4.1 (secure configuration process)** to be the single most effective Safeguard across all five attack types.

blocks.title: Read the numbers carefully
blocks.text: "Defends against" means at least one Safeguard mitigates the technique, not that the attack is impossible. The model assumes Safeguards are fully and correctly implemented. Use CDM to justify priorities, not to promise immunity.

items: **Claiming an IG you haven't evidenced.** An IG is achieved when every Safeguard in it is implemented and can be shown, not when most are.
**Jumping to IG3 tools before IG1 basics.** An expensive NDR platform does little if you don't know what assets you have.
**Treating IG as a maturity score.** IGs describe which Safeguards apply, not how well they are done. Use CSAT or your own scale for maturity.
**Ignoring the Govern Safeguards.** Policies and processes (e.g. 3.1, 4.1, 7.1, 8.1, 11.1) are what make technical controls repeatable and auditable.

quiz.explain: IGs are cumulative: 56 + 74 = 130.

chapters.title: Controls 1-3: Know what you have
chapters.summary: Enterprise assets, software assets and data protection: 26 Safeguards.

sections.title: Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets

blocks.text: Actively manage every enterprise asset (end-user devices, servers, network gear, IoT and OT devices) whether physical, virtual, remote or in the cloud, so you know exactly what you must protect and can spot and remove anything unauthorised.
Why it matters

You cannot patch, configure, monitor or recover what you don't know exists. Attackers scan continuously for forgotten test servers, unmanaged laptops and shadow cloud instances. Control 1 is the foundation that most other Controls depend on.

blocks.title: Where to start
blocks.text: Pull asset lists from what you already run: Active Directory or Entra ID, the MDM, the EDR console, DHCP servers, cloud provider inventories and the finance fixed-asset register. Reconcile them. The gaps between those lists are your first findings.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain Detailed Enterprise Asset Inventory.** Keep an accurate, detailed and current inventory of every enterprise asset that can store or process data: end-user devices (including mobile), network devices, IoT/non-computing devices and servers, on-premises and in the cloud. Record at least network and hardware addresses, machine name, owner, department and whether it is approved to connect. Review twice a year or more often.
blocks.practice: Use a CMDB or asset management tool fed automatically by discovery sources (MDM, EDR, directory, cloud APIs). Evidence: the inventory export with owner and approval fields populated, and a record of the last review.
blocks.example: A retail chain reconciles its MDM, EDR and DHCP data and finds 180 point-of-sale terminals missing from the CMDB, including 12 still running an unsupported OS.

blocks.text: **Address Unauthorized Assets.** Have a process to deal with unauthorised assets at least weekly: remove them from the network, deny remote connection, or quarantine them.
blocks.practice: Define who reviews the unauthorised-asset report, the decision options and the timeline. Network access control (NAC) or switch-port shutdown can automate quarantine.
blocks.example: A personal Raspberry Pi appears on a branch network; the weekly review flags it and the port is shut down the same day.

blocks.text: **Utilize an Active Discovery Tool.** Run an active discovery tool that scans the network to find connected assets, daily or more often.
blocks.practice: Use network scanners or the discovery module of your vulnerability scanner; scan all subnets including VPN pools and cloud VPCs. Feed results into the inventory (1.1).
blocks.example: Nightly scans at a university reveal a lab server nobody registered, exposing an old database on the campus network.

blocks.text: **Use Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Logging to Update Enterprise Asset Inventory.** Use DHCP server logs or IP address management (IPAM) tools to update the asset inventory, reviewing them weekly or more often.
blocks.practice: Forward DHCP lease logs to the SIEM or CMDB and alert on MAC addresses not in the inventory.
blocks.example: DHCP logs show a new device requesting leases every night at 2 a.m.; it turns out to be a contractor's unmanaged laptop left in a meeting room.

blocks.text: **Use a Passive Asset Discovery Tool.** Use a passive discovery tool (listening to network traffic rather than scanning) to identify connected assets, and use the results to update the inventory at least weekly.
blocks.practice: Network detection and response (NDR) or OT passive monitoring tools are common choices, especially where active scanning could disrupt fragile devices.
blocks.example: A gas processing plant uses passive OT monitoring because active scans once crashed a PLC; it discovers 40 undocumented field devices.

sections.title: Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

blocks.text: Actively manage all software (operating systems and applications) so that only authorised, supported software is installed and allowed to run, and unauthorised or unmanaged software is found and removed.
Why it matters

Unsupported and unknown software carries unpatched vulnerabilities; unauthorised tools are a common route for malware and data leakage. Allowlisting is one of the strongest defences against ransomware because unknown executables simply cannot run.

blocks.title: Allowlisting takes planning
blocks.text: Application allowlisting (2.5-2.7) breaks things if rolled out cold. Start in audit mode, build the allowlist from observed usage, then enforce on high-risk groups first (servers, admin workstations, OT engineering stations).
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Software Inventory.** Keep a detailed inventory of all licensed software on enterprise assets: title, publisher, install or first-use date and business purpose, and where useful the URL, app store, version, deployment method and decommission date. Review twice a year or more often.
blocks.practice: Combine software inventory from endpoint management, SaaS discovery (CASB or SSO logs) and procurement records. Evidence: inventory with business purpose filled in.
blocks.example: An insurer's inventory shows three different PDF editors across departments; it standardises on one and removes the others.

blocks.text: **Ensure Authorized Software is Currently Supported.** Only software that the vendor still supports may be authorised. If unsupported software is essential, document an exception with compensating controls and risk acceptance; otherwise treat it as unauthorised. Check support status at least monthly.
blocks.practice: Track end-of-life dates in the inventory and create exceptions with an expiry date and an owner.
blocks.example: A hospital must keep an imaging system on an unsupported OS; it documents an exception, isolates the device on its own VLAN and restricts access to two technicians.

blocks.text: **Address Unauthorized Software.** Remove unauthorised software from enterprise assets or give it a documented exception. Review at least monthly.
blocks.practice: Report on software not in the authorised list and remove it via endpoint management; track exceptions.
blocks.example: Monthly reporting finds a remote-access tool installed by a vendor without approval; it is removed and the vendor's access moved to the approved gateway.

blocks.text: **Utilize Automated Software Inventory Tools.** Use software inventory tools wherever possible to discover and document installed software automatically.
blocks.practice: Endpoint management (e.g. Intune, SCCM, Jamf), EDR inventories and cloud workload agents usually cover this.
blocks.example: A manufacturer replaces a yearly manual software survey with automated inventory from its endpoint agent, updated daily.

blocks.text: **Allowlist Authorized Software.** Use technical controls such as application allowlisting so that only authorised software can run. Reassess twice a year or more often.
blocks.practice: Windows App Control (WDAC) or AppLocker, macOS management profiles, or EDR application control. Start in audit mode.
blocks.example: A payment processor enforces allowlisting on its card-environment servers; a ransomware binary dropped by an attacker fails to execute.

blocks.text: **Allowlist Authorized Libraries.** Ensure only authorised software libraries (such as .dll, .so or .ocx files) can load into a process, and block the rest. Reassess twice a year or more often.
blocks.practice: Use code-integrity policies that cover libraries and require signed modules.
blocks.example: App Control blocks an unsigned DLL side-loaded next to a legitimate application during a red-team exercise.

blocks.text: **Allowlist Authorized Scripts.** Use technical controls such as digital signatures and version control so that only authorised scripts (e.g. .ps1, .py) can run, and block unauthorised ones. Reassess twice a year or more often.
blocks.practice: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode with signed-script requirements; restrict interpreters on servers.
blocks.example: Only scripts signed by the IT automation team's certificate can run on domain controllers.

blocks.text: Develop processes and technical controls to identify, classify, securely handle, retain and dispose of data throughout its lifecycle.
Why it matters

Data is what attackers monetise, and what regulators fine you for losing. Since v8 the Controls are data-centric: protect the data wherever it lives (on-premises, SaaS, cloud, end-user devices), not just the network perimeter.

blocks.title: Executive view
blocks.text: Data protection is where cybersecurity meets privacy law. Controls 3.1-3.5 (all IG1) give you the minimum evidence regulators expect under laws such as GDPR, the Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017 or Saudi PDPL: you know what personal data you hold, who can access it, how long you keep it and how you destroy it.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Data Management Process.** Establish and maintain a data management process that covers data sensitivity, data owners, handling, retention limits and disposal requirements. Review it annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: A data management or information handling policy and procedure, approved by management, with named data owners.
blocks.example: A telecom operator's data management standard assigns owners to subscriber, billing and network data, each with retention and disposal rules.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Data Inventory.** Keep a data inventory based on the data management process, covering sensitive data at a minimum. Review it at least annually, prioritising sensitive data.
blocks.practice: Record data sets, location (system, SaaS, cloud), owner and classification. Data discovery tools help find sensitive data you didn't know about.
blocks.example: A discovery scan finds national ID numbers in 3,000 files on a shared drive at an insurer, which are then moved to a controlled repository.

blocks.text: **Configure Data Access Control Lists.** Configure data access control lists (permissions) based on need to know, on local and remote file systems, databases and applications.
blocks.practice: Group-based permissions, no "Everyone" or public links on sensitive stores, periodic permission reviews.
blocks.example: An access review removes 1,400 users from a finance share that had inherited broad permissions years earlier.

blocks.text: **Enforce Data Retention.** Retain data according to the data management process, with both minimum and maximum retention periods.
blocks.practice: Implement retention labels and policies in email, file stores and databases; purge data past its maximum.
blocks.example: A bank keeps transaction records for the legally required period, then automatically deletes them rather than keeping them forever.

blocks.text: **Securely Dispose of Data.** Dispose of data securely, as the data management process defines, using methods appropriate to the data's sensitivity.
blocks.practice: Crypto-erase or wipe to NIST SP 800-88, shred paper, obtain destruction certificates from disposal vendors.
blocks.example: Retired laptops are wiped and the disposal vendor provides serial-number-level destruction certificates.

blocks.text: **Encrypt Data on End-User Devices.** Encrypt data on end-user devices that hold sensitive data, for example with BitLocker, FileVault or dm-crypt.
blocks.practice: Enforce full-disk encryption through device management and escrow recovery keys centrally. Evidence: compliance report showing encrypted devices.
blocks.example: A stolen sales laptop becomes a non-event because BitLocker was enforced and the recovery key was held in Entra ID.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Data Classification Scheme.** Establish and maintain a data classification scheme (for example Sensitive, Confidential, Public) and classify data accordingly. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Keep the scheme simple (three or four levels), train staff, and apply labels in tools where possible.
blocks.example: A government agency adopts Public, Internal, Confidential and Secret labels, applied automatically to documents containing personal data.

blocks.text: **Document Data Flows.** Document data flows, including flows to and from service providers, based on the data management process. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Data flow diagrams for key processes and systems; include SaaS and API integrations.
blocks.example: Mapping data flows for a loan origination system reveals that applicant data is sent to an unvetted credit-scoring API.

blocks.text: **Encrypt Data on Removable Media.** Encrypt data stored on removable media such as USB drives and external disks, so a lost or stolen device doesn't expose it.
blocks.practice: Enforce encryption (e.g. BitLocker To Go) or block writes to unencrypted USB storage.
blocks.example: Staff can copy files to USB drives only if the drive is encrypted; unencrypted drives are read-only.

blocks.text: **Encrypt Sensitive Data in Transit.** Encrypt sensitive data in transit, for example with TLS or SSH.
blocks.practice: Disable legacy protocols (TLS 1.0/1.1, FTP, Telnet); use TLS 1.2+ for internal as well as external traffic.
blocks.example: An internal HR API moves from HTTP to mutual TLS after a network capture shows salaries in plain text.

blocks.text: **Encrypt Sensitive Data at Rest.** Encrypt sensitive data at rest on servers, applications and databases. Storage-level (server-side) encryption meets the minimum; application-level (client-side) encryption goes further by keeping plain text away from anyone with storage access.
blocks.practice: Database TDE, cloud storage encryption with customer-managed keys, application-level field encryption for the most sensitive fields.
blocks.example: A SaaS provider encrypts customer PII columns at application level so that database administrators cannot read them.

blocks.text: **Segment Data Processing and Storage Based on Sensitivity.** Segment data processing and storage by sensitivity; don't process sensitive data on assets meant for lower-sensitivity data.
blocks.practice: Separate networks, subscriptions or accounts for sensitive workloads; restrict flows between zones.
blocks.example: Cardholder data lives in a separate cloud account and network segment, reducing PCI DSS scope.

blocks.text: **Deploy a Data Loss Prevention Solution.** Implement an automated tool, such as host-based data loss prevention (DLP), to identify sensitive data stored, processed or transmitted by enterprise assets, including at service providers, and update the sensitive data inventory.
blocks.practice: DLP across endpoints, email, cloud storage and SaaS, tuned to your data types.
blocks.example: DLP blocks an employee from uploading a customer list to a personal cloud drive and alerts the security team.

blocks.text: **Log Sensitive Data Access.** Log access to sensitive data, including modification and disposal.
blocks.practice: Enable object-level audit logging on sensitive file stores and databases; send logs to the SIEM.
blocks.example: Database audit logs show an administrator querying VIP customer records outside business hours, triggering an investigation.
