sections.title: Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

blocks.text: Establish and maintain secure configurations for enterprise assets (end-user devices, servers, network devices, IoT) and software (operating systems and applications).
Why it matters

Default settings favour ease of deployment, not security: default passwords, open services, legacy protocols. Secure configuration shrinks the attack surface and is where the CIS Benchmarks plug directly into the Controls.

blocks.title: The Benchmark connection
blocks.text: Safeguard 4.1 asks for a secure configuration process. CIS Benchmarks (and CIS Hardened Images) are the most common way to meet it: pick the Benchmark for each platform, choose a profile, document deviations, and measure drift. The CIS Community Defense Model found 4.1 the single most effective Safeguard across the attack types it analysed.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Secure Configuration Process.** Establish and maintain a secure configuration process for enterprise assets (end-user devices, IoT, servers) and software (operating systems and applications). Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Adopt CIS Benchmarks (or STIGs) as baselines, document approved deviations, deploy through tooling and measure compliance.
blocks.example: An enterprise adopts CIS Level 1 for Windows 11 and Ubuntu, documents 14 deviations, and reports monthly compliance by business unit.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Secure Configuration Process for Network Infrastructure.** Establish and maintain a secure configuration process for network devices. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Configuration standards for routers, switches, firewalls and wireless, based on vendor hardening guides or CIS Benchmarks for network devices.
blocks.example: A standard for all Cisco devices disables unused services, enforces SSH and AAA, and is checked by an automated config audit.

blocks.text: **Configure Automatic Session Locking on Enterprise Assets.** Configure automatic session locking after a period of inactivity: no more than 15 minutes on general-purpose operating systems and no more than 2 minutes on mobile devices.
blocks.practice: Enforce via GPO, Intune or MDM profiles; verify through compliance reports.
blocks.example: A hospital sets a 10-minute lock on shared workstations and uses tap-badge re-authentication so clinicians can unlock quickly.

blocks.text: **Implement and Manage a Firewall on Servers.** Implement and manage a firewall on servers where supported: a virtual firewall, the OS firewall or a third-party agent.
blocks.practice: Default-deny inbound rules per server role, managed centrally; cloud security groups count for cloud servers.
blocks.example: Server firewall rules allow database traffic only from the application tier, blocking lateral movement from user networks.

blocks.text: **Implement and Manage a Firewall on End-User Devices.** Implement and manage a host-based firewall or port-filtering tool on end-user devices, with a default-deny rule that drops all traffic except explicitly allowed services and ports.
blocks.practice: Enable Windows Defender Firewall or equivalent via policy; block inbound SMB and RDP on laptops.
blocks.example: Blocking inbound SMB on laptops stops a worm from spreading across the office Wi-Fi.

blocks.text: **Securely Manage Enterprise Assets and Software.** Manage enterprise assets and software securely, for example through version-controlled infrastructure as code and administration over secure protocols such as SSH and HTTPS. Avoid insecure protocols like Telnet and HTTP unless operationally essential.
blocks.practice: Use IaC pipelines with peer review; disable Telnet/HTTP management interfaces.
blocks.example: A SaaS company manages all cloud infrastructure through Terraform with pull-request approval, so manual console changes are rare and auditable.

blocks.text: **Manage Default Accounts on Enterprise Assets and Software.** Manage default accounts such as root, administrator and vendor-preconfigured accounts, for example by disabling them or making them unusable.
blocks.practice: Rename or disable built-in accounts, change default passwords at build time, and check new devices before deployment.
blocks.example: A penetration test finds a CCTV system still using the vendor's default admin password; the build checklist is updated to catch this.

blocks.text: **Uninstall or Disable Unnecessary Services on Enterprise Assets and Software.** Uninstall or disable unnecessary services on enterprise assets and software, such as unused file-sharing services, web application modules or service functions.
blocks.practice: Use Benchmark recommendations to identify unnecessary services; build role-based images.
blocks.example: Removing the unused print spooler service from domain controllers eliminates a class of privilege-escalation vulnerabilities.

blocks.text: **Configure Trusted DNS Servers on Enterprise Assets.** Configure enterprise assets to use trusted DNS servers: enterprise-controlled ones and/or reputable external resolvers.
blocks.practice: Push DNS settings via DHCP and device management; block outbound DNS to unapproved resolvers.
blocks.example: Blocking outbound port 53 except to the corporate resolvers stops malware using its own DNS servers.

blocks.text: **Enforce Automatic Device Lockout on Portable End-User Devices.** Lock portable end-user devices after a set number of failed local login attempts, where supported: no more than 20 attempts for laptops and no more than 10 for tablets and smartphones.
blocks.practice: Configure lockout via Intune, Jamf or MDM configuration profiles.
blocks.example: Company phones wipe or lock after 10 failed passcode attempts, as configured in the MDM profile.

blocks.text: **Enforce Remote Wipe Capability on Portable End-User Devices.** Be able to remotely wipe enterprise data from enterprise-owned portable devices when appropriate, such as when lost, stolen or when a person leaves.
blocks.practice: Enable remote wipe or selective wipe through MDM; include it in the leaver and lost-device procedures.
blocks.example: A lost tablet is selectively wiped within an hour of the loss being reported to the service desk.

blocks.text: **Separate Enterprise Workspaces on Mobile End-User Devices.** Use separate enterprise workspaces on mobile devices where supported, for example Apple configuration profiles or Android Work Profile, to separate enterprise apps and data from personal ones.
blocks.practice: BYOD with work profiles and app protection policies so corporate data can't be pasted into personal apps.
blocks.example: Staff use their own phones for email through a work profile; leaving the company removes only the work profile.

blocks.text: Use processes and tools to assign and manage credentials for user, administrator and service accounts across enterprise assets and software.
Why it matters
Valid credentials are the attacker's favourite way in, because logging in looks normal. Orphaned, shared, default and over-privileged accounts turn one phished password into a full compromise.

blocks.title: Service accounts
blocks.text: Service accounts are often the most privileged and least watched accounts in the estate: no MFA, passwords that never change, nobody owns them. Safeguard 5.5 exists for that reason.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Accounts.** Keep an inventory of all user and administrator accounts, including at least the person's name, username, start and stop dates and department. Validate that all active accounts are authorised at least quarterly.
blocks.practice: Export accounts from directories and key applications; reconcile with HR records each quarter.
blocks.example: A quarterly reconciliation with HR finds 37 active accounts belonging to people who left in the past year.

blocks.text: **Use Unique Passwords.** Use unique passwords for all enterprise assets. Good practice is at least 8 characters for accounts protected by MFA and at least 14 characters for accounts without MFA.
blocks.practice: Password policy in the directory, a password manager for staff, and unique local admin passwords (e.g. Windows LAPS).
blocks.example: Windows LAPS gives every workstation a unique local administrator password, so one stolen hash no longer unlocks every PC.

blocks.text: **Disable Dormant Accounts.** Delete or disable accounts that have been inactive for 45 days, where supported.
blocks.practice: Automated dormant-account reports and disablement; handle exceptions (e.g. staff on long leave) explicitly.
blocks.example: A script disables accounts inactive for 45 days and notifies the manager, who can request reactivation.

blocks.text: **Restrict Administrator Privileges to Dedicated Administrator Accounts.** Give administrator privileges only to dedicated administrator accounts. Do everyday work (browsing, email, office apps) from a separate non-privileged account.
blocks.practice: Separate admin accounts (e.g. adm-jdoe), no mailbox or internet access for admin accounts, removal of local admin from standard users.
blocks.example: After removing local admin rights from staff, a phishing payload fails to install persistence on the user's laptop.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Accounts.** Keep an inventory of service accounts with at least the owning department, review date and purpose. Review at least quarterly that all active service accounts are authorised.
blocks.practice: Tag service accounts in the directory, assign owners, and move them into a PAM vault or use managed identities.
blocks.example: An inventory of 420 service accounts reveals 90 with no owner; 60 are disabled after owners confirm they are unused.

blocks.text: **Centralize Account Management.** Centralise account management through a directory or identity service.
blocks.practice: Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta or similar as the single source for identities; connect applications through SSO and provisioning.
blocks.example: Connecting 40 SaaS apps to the identity provider means disabling one account now removes access everywhere.

blocks.text: Use processes and tools to create, assign, manage and revoke access credentials and privileges for user, administrator and service accounts.
Why it matters

Control 5 manages the accounts; Control 6 manages what those accounts can do. MFA (6.3-6.5) alone blocks the vast majority of credential-stuffing and password-spray attacks, which is why three MFA Safeguards sit in IG1.

blocks.title: Quick win
blocks.text: If you can fund only one identity project this year, make it MFA on all externally-exposed applications, remote access and administrative access (6.3, 6.4, 6.5). It is cheap relative to the risk it removes and insurers increasingly require it.
Safeguards
**Establish an Access Granting Process.** Establish and follow a process, preferably automated, for granting access when someone joins, is granted new rights or changes role.
blocks.practice: Joiner and mover workflows driven by HR events, with manager approval and role-based access packages.
blocks.example: A new branch employee receives a standard teller access package on day one, approved by the branch manager.

blocks.text: **Establish an Access Revoking Process.** Establish and follow a process, preferably automated, for revoking access: disable accounts immediately on termination, rights revocation or role change. Disabling rather than deleting may be needed to keep audit trails.
blocks.practice: HR-triggered leaver workflow that disables all accounts the same day; mover workflow removes old role access.
blocks.example: A dismissed employee's access is disabled within 15 minutes of HR recording the termination.

blocks.text: **Require MFA for Externally-Exposed Applications.** Require MFA for all externally-exposed enterprise and third-party applications where supported. Enforcing MFA through a directory service or SSO provider satisfies this.
blocks.practice: Conditional access policies in the identity provider covering all internet-facing apps, including SaaS.
blocks.example: Requiring MFA on the webmail and HR portal stops a password-spray campaign that had already guessed 12 passwords.

blocks.text: **Require MFA for Remote Network Access.** Require MFA whenever someone connects to the enterprise network remotely, for example through VPN, virtual desktop or remote desktop gateways.
blocks.practice: VPN, VDI and remote-access gateways all require MFA.
blocks.example: The VPN is integrated with the identity provider and requires number-matching push approval.

blocks.text: **Require MFA for Administrative Access.** Require MFA for all administrative accounts where supported, on all assets, whether managed on-site or by a third party.
blocks.practice: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2, smart cards) for admins, including cloud console and MSP accounts.
blocks.example: Cloud root and global admin accounts require hardware security keys held in a safe.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Authentication and Authorization Systems.** Keep an inventory of the enterprise's authentication and authorisation systems, on-site and at service providers. Review at least annually.
blocks.practice: List directories, identity providers, PAM tools, and applications with their own local authentication.
blocks.example: The inventory shows five applications still using local logins; they are prioritised for SSO integration.

blocks.text: **Centralize Access Control.** Centralise access control for all enterprise assets through a directory service or SSO provider where supported.
blocks.practice: SSO for applications, directory-based authorisation groups, and fewer local accounts.
blocks.example: Moving the ERP to SSO means access reviews happen in one place instead of per application.

blocks.text: **Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control.** Define and maintain role-based access control by documenting the access each role needs. Review access to validate all privileges at least annually.
blocks.practice: Role catalogue mapped to entitlements; certification campaigns for access reviews; separation of duties rules.
blocks.example: A role model for the finance department reduces 300 unique permission combinations to 12 roles with clear owners.

quiz.q: What is the maximum inactivity before automatic session lock on a general-purpose OS (4.3)?
quiz.explain: 15 minutes for general-purpose OS; 2 minutes for mobile devices.

quiz.q: After how many days of inactivity should dormant accounts be disabled (5.3)?
quiz.explain: 45 days, where supported.

quiz.q: Good practice password length for accounts without MFA under 5.2 is at least...
quiz.explain: 14 characters without MFA; 8 characters with MFA.

quiz.q: Which three MFA Safeguards are in IG1?
quiz.explain: MFA for externally-exposed apps (6.3), remote network access (6.4) and administrative access (6.5).

quiz.q: How many failed login attempts may a laptop allow before lockout under 4.10?
quiz.explain: No more than 20 for laptops, no more than 10 for tablets and smartphones.

quiz.q: Role-based access control (6.8) is in which IG?
quiz.explain: 6.8 is IG3.

chapters.title: Controls 7-10: Fix, watch and filter
chapters.summary: Vulnerability management, audit logs, email and web protections, malware defences: 33 Safeguards.

blocks.text: Continuously assess and track vulnerabilities across enterprise assets, and remediate them to minimise the window of opportunity for attackers. Monitor public and private sources for new threat and vulnerability information.
Why it matters
Exploiting known, unpatched vulnerabilities remains one of the most common initial access routes. The race is between the time a fix is published and the time attackers weaponise it, often days.

blocks.title: Risk-based, not CVSS-only
blocks.text: Prioritise by exploitability and exposure (for example CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, EPSS scores, internet-facing assets) rather than CVSS score alone. A medium-severity bug being actively exploited on your VPN beats a critical one on an isolated lab server.
Safeguards
**Establish and Maintain a Vulnerability Management Process.** Establish and maintain a documented vulnerability management process for enterprise assets. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: A documented process covering scope, scanning, prioritisation, remediation SLAs, exceptions and reporting.
blocks.example: A bank's process sets remediation SLAs of 7 days for exploited internet-facing vulnerabilities, 30 days for critical internal ones.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Remediation Process.** Establish and maintain a risk-based remediation strategy in a documented remediation process, reviewed monthly or more often.
blocks.practice: Define prioritisation criteria (exposure, exploitation, asset criticality), owners and exception handling.
blocks.example: Monthly remediation reviews focus the server team on the 40 vulnerabilities that are internet-facing and actively exploited, rather than 9,000 findings.

blocks.text: **Perform Automated Operating System Patch Management.** Update operating systems on enterprise assets through automated patch management monthly or more often.
blocks.practice: Windows Update for Business, WSUS, Intune, Jamf, or Linux package automation; report patch compliance.
blocks.example: Automated monthly OS patching with a pilot ring raises compliance from 62% to 96% in a quarter.

blocks.text: **Perform Automated Application Patch Management.** Update applications on enterprise assets through automated patch management monthly or more often.
blocks.practice: Third-party patching tools or packaging for common apps (browsers, PDF readers, Java, collaboration tools).
blocks.example: Automated patching of browsers and PDF readers closes the gap attackers used in a previous drive-by compromise.

blocks.text: **Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Internal Enterprise Assets.** Run automated vulnerability scans of internal assets quarterly or more often, including both authenticated and unauthenticated scans, using a SCAP-compliant scanner.
blocks.practice: Authenticated scans (with credentials) find missing patches and misconfigurations that unauthenticated scans miss.
blocks.example: Switching to authenticated scans reveals 3x more missing patches on servers than unauthenticated scans had shown.

blocks.text: **Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Externally-Exposed Enterprise Assets.** Run automated vulnerability scans of externally-exposed assets monthly or more often using a SCAP-compliant scanner.
blocks.practice: External scanning plus attack surface management to find forgotten internet-facing assets.
blocks.example: External scans find a forgotten marketing microsite running an outdated CMS with a known remote code execution flaw.

blocks.text: **Remediate Detected Vulnerabilities.** Remediate detected software vulnerabilities through processes and tooling monthly or more often, based on the remediation process.
blocks.practice: Track findings to closure in a ticketing system; measure mean time to remediate by severity.
blocks.example: The team tracks vulnerabilities as tickets with SLA timers, and reports mean time to remediate to the risk committee.

blocks.text: Collect, alert on, review and retain audit logs of events that could help detect, understand or recover from an attack.
Why it matters

Without logs you cannot detect an intrusion, determine its scope or prove what happened to regulators and insurers. Attackers often sit undetected for weeks because logging was off, not centralised or never reviewed.

blocks.title: Logs nobody reads
blocks.text: Collecting logs (8.2) is IG1; reviewing them (8.11) is IG2. Collecting without reviewing gives you forensic evidence after the fact, but not detection. Budget for the people or managed service that will look at them.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain an Audit Log Management Process.** Establish and maintain an audit log management process defining the enterprise's logging requirements, covering at least collection, review and retention. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: A logging standard listing which systems log what, where logs go, how long they're kept and who reviews them.
blocks.example: The logging standard requires authentication, admin actions and security events from all Tier 1 systems to go to the SIEM.

blocks.text: **Collect Audit Logs.** Collect audit logs: make sure logging, as the log management process requires, is enabled across enterprise assets.
blocks.practice: Enable OS, application, cloud and SaaS audit logs; verify that each Tier 1 system is sending logs.
blocks.example: Turning on Microsoft 365 unified audit logging lets the team investigate a mailbox compromise that would otherwise be invisible.

blocks.text: **Ensure Adequate Audit Log Storage.** Make sure log destinations have enough storage to meet the log management process.
blocks.practice: Capacity monitoring on log storage and SIEM ingestion; alerts before logs roll over.
blocks.example: An investigation fails because firewall logs rolled over after 3 days; storage is expanded and monitored.

blocks.text: **Standardize Time Synchronization.** Standardise time synchronisation: configure at least two synchronised time sources across enterprise assets where supported.
blocks.practice: Use internal NTP servers synced to reliable sources; accurate timestamps are essential for correlating events.
blocks.example: Correlating an attack timeline is easy because all systems use the same NTP sources and UTC timestamps.

blocks.text: **Collect Detailed Audit Logs.** Configure detailed audit logging for assets holding sensitive data: event source, date, username, timestamp, source and destination addresses, and other details useful for forensics.
blocks.practice: Advanced audit policies on servers, database auditing and application logs with user context.
blocks.example: Detailed logs on the customer database show exactly which records an attacker queried, limiting the breach notification scope.

blocks.text: **Collect DNS Query Audit Logs.** Collect DNS query logs on enterprise assets where appropriate and supported.
blocks.practice: DNS server or resolver logs, or DNS security service logs, sent to the SIEM.
blocks.example: DNS logs reveal a workstation querying a known command-and-control domain every 60 seconds.

blocks.text: **Collect URL Request Audit Logs.** Collect URL request logs on enterprise assets where appropriate and supported.
blocks.practice: Proxy, secure web gateway or firewall URL logs.
blocks.example: Proxy logs show which users visited a compromised supplier website during the attack window.

blocks.text: **Collect Command-Line Audit Logs.** Collect command-line audit logs, for example from PowerShell, Bash and remote administrative terminals.
blocks.practice: PowerShell script block logging, process creation with command line, and Linux auditd rules.
blocks.example: PowerShell logs capture an attacker's encoded command that downloads a ransomware loader.

blocks.text: **Centralize Audit Logs.** Centralise audit log collection and retention across enterprise assets as far as possible.
blocks.practice: A SIEM or log analytics platform; protect it from tampering.
blocks.example: Centralised logs survive even though the attacker cleared local event logs on compromised servers.

blocks.text: **Retain Audit Logs.** Retain audit logs across enterprise assets for at least 90 days.
blocks.practice: Hot storage for 90 days and cold storage for longer periods required by regulation or incident response.
blocks.example: An intrusion discovered 70 days after it began can still be investigated because logs are retained for a year.

blocks.text: **Conduct Audit Log Reviews.** Review audit logs to detect anomalies or abnormal events that could indicate a threat, weekly or more often.
blocks.practice: Automated correlation plus analyst review; for smaller teams, a managed detection service.
blocks.example: Weekly review of failed-login trends reveals a slow password-spray attack against the VPN.

blocks.text: **Collect Service Provider Logs.** Collect service provider logs where supported, such as authentication and authorisation events, data creation and disposal, and user management events.
blocks.practice: Ingest SaaS and cloud audit logs via API; negotiate log access in contracts.
blocks.example: Salesforce and cloud provider audit logs flow into the SIEM, showing a mass data export by a compromised account.

sections.title: Control 9: Email and Web Browser Protections

blocks.text: Improve protections and detections against threats arriving through email and web browsers, where attackers manipulate human behaviour.
Why it matters
Email and web browsing are the two most common ways malware and credential phishing reach users. These Safeguards filter threats before a person has to make a decision.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A company implements DNS filtering (9.2), DMARC at p=reject (9.5) and blocks executable attachments (9.6). Phishing reaching inboxes drops sharply, and spoofed emails using its own domain stop being delivered to customers.
Safeguards
**Ensure Use of Only Fully Supported Browsers and Email Clients.** Allow only fully supported browsers and email clients to run, using the latest vendor versions.
blocks.practice: Standardise browsers, enforce auto-update, and remove legacy browsers.
blocks.example: Removing Internet Explorer and enforcing auto-updating Edge and Chrome eliminates a class of legacy exploits.

blocks.text: **Use DNS Filtering Services.** Use DNS filtering services on all enterprise assets to block access to known malicious domains.
blocks.practice: Protective DNS services, including for remote users via agents.
blocks.example: Protective DNS blocks a user from reaching a phishing site impersonating the company's payroll portal.

blocks.text: **Maintain and Enforce Network-Based URL Filters.** Enforce and update network-based URL filters to stop assets connecting to potentially malicious or unapproved websites, using category, reputation or block lists, for all assets.
blocks.practice: Secure web gateway or firewall URL filtering, including roaming users.
blocks.example: Category filtering blocks newly registered domains, a common source of phishing and malware.

blocks.text: **Restrict Unnecessary or Unauthorized Browser and Email Client Extensions.** Remove or disable unauthorised or unnecessary browser and email client plugins, extensions and add-ons.
blocks.practice: Allowlist extensions through browser management policies.
blocks.example: An extension allowlist stops a malicious "PDF converter" extension that was harvesting session cookies.

blocks.text: **Implement DMARC.** Implement DMARC policy and verification, starting with SPF and DKIM, to reduce spoofed or modified email from valid domains.
blocks.practice: Publish SPF and DKIM, then DMARC starting at p=none with reporting, moving to quarantine and reject.
blocks.example: Moving DMARC to p=reject stops fraudsters sending invoice emails that appear to come from the company's own domain.

blocks.text: **Block Unnecessary File Types.** Block unnecessary file types attempting to enter through the email gateway.
blocks.practice: Block executables, scripts, macro-enabled documents from external senders and unusual archive types.
blocks.example: Blocking .iso, .js and .hta attachments cuts malware reaching users by more than half.

blocks.text: **Deploy and Maintain Email Server Anti-Malware Protections.** Deploy and maintain email server anti-malware protections such as attachment scanning and sandboxing.
blocks.practice: Email security with attachment detonation and URL rewriting.
blocks.example: Sandboxing detonates a weaponised document that signature scanning missed and quarantines it before delivery.

blocks.text: Prevent or control the installation, spread and execution of malicious applications, code or scripts on enterprise assets.
Why it matters
Malware, including ransomware, remains the payload of most attacks. Modern anti-malware (EDR and next-generation antivirus) combines signatures, behaviour analysis and exploit prevention.

blocks.title: Built-in is often enough to start
blocks.text: Microsoft Defender, macOS XProtect and Gatekeeper, and Linux tooling cover 10.1-10.3 for IG1 at little extra cost. The key is central management (10.6) so you know every device is protected and up to date.
Safeguards
**Deploy and Maintain Anti-Malware Software.** Deploy anti-malware software on every enterprise asset, endpoints and servers alike, and keep it running and maintained.
blocks.practice: EDR or next-generation antivirus on endpoints and servers; verify coverage against the asset inventory.
blocks.example: Comparing the EDR console to the asset inventory reveals 60 servers with no protection agent.

blocks.text: **Configure Automatic Anti-Malware Signature Updates.** Make sure anti-malware signature updates happen automatically on all assets, without relying on users.
blocks.practice: Automatic updates enabled and monitored centrally.
blocks.example: The console alerts when any device's signatures are more than 3 days old.

blocks.text: **Disable Autorun and Autoplay for Removable Media.** Turn off autorun and autoplay so that inserting removable media never runs its content automatically.
blocks.practice: Group Policy or MDM settings disabling AutoRun and AutoPlay (a standard CIS Benchmark recommendation).
blocks.example: An infected USB stick dropped in a car park fails to execute automatically when plugged in.

blocks.text: **Configure Automatic Anti-Malware Scanning of Removable Media.** Set anti-malware software to scan removable media automatically as soon as it is connected.
blocks.practice: Enable scanning on mount for USB and external drives.
blocks.example: A contractor's USB drive is scanned on insertion and a worm is quarantined.

blocks.text: **Enable Anti-Exploitation Features.** Enable anti-exploitation features where possible, such as Data Execution Prevention, Windows Defender Exploit Guard, or Apple System Integrity Protection and Gatekeeper.
blocks.practice: Enable exploit protection and attack surface reduction rules; test in audit mode first.
blocks.example: An attack surface reduction rule blocks Office from spawning child processes, stopping a macro-based attack.

blocks.text: **Centrally Manage Anti-Malware Software.** Manage anti-malware from a central console so that policy, updates, alerts and coverage are controlled and visible in one place.
blocks.practice: Single console for policy, alerting and health; integrate alerts with the SIEM.
blocks.example: Central management reveals that a group of branch PCs had their protection disabled by a local technician.

blocks.text: **Use Behavior-Based Anti-Malware Software.** Use anti-malware that detects malicious behaviour, such as credential theft or mass file encryption, not only known signatures.
blocks.practice: EDR with behavioural detection of techniques such as credential dumping and mass encryption.
blocks.example: EDR detects and kills a process encrypting files at high speed before it spreads beyond one share.

quiz.q: How often should internal vulnerability scans run under 7.5?
quiz.explain: Quarterly or more often, authenticated and unauthenticated. External scans (7.6) are monthly.

quiz.q: What is the minimum audit log retention in 8.10?
quiz.explain: 90 days minimum.

quiz.q: Standardised time synchronisation (8.4) requires at least...
options: A GPS clock on every server
quiz.explain: At least two synchronised time sources, where supported.

quiz.q: DMARC is covered by which Safeguard?
quiz.explain: 9.5 Implement DMARC, starting with SPF and DKIM.

quiz.q: Which Safeguard is IG1?
quiz.explain: 9.2 is IG1. The others are IG2.

quiz.q: How often should OS patching run under 7.3?
quiz.explain: Automated OS patch management monthly or more often.

chapters.title: Controls 11-13: Recover and defend the network
chapters.summary: Data recovery, network infrastructure and network monitoring: 24 Safeguards.

blocks.text: Establish and maintain data recovery practices sufficient to restore in-scope enterprise assets to a pre-incident, trusted state.
Why it matters
Backups are the last line of defence against ransomware, destructive attacks and mistakes. Attackers now deliberately target backups first, which is why isolation (11.4) is in IG1.

blocks.title: Untested backups are hope, not recovery
blocks.text: Many organisations discover during a ransomware attack that backups were incomplete, encrypted too, or took weeks to restore. Test restores (11.5) against your recovery time objectives.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Data Recovery Process.** Establish and maintain a data recovery process covering the scope of recovery, recovery priorities and the security of backup data. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Documented backup and recovery process aligned with business impact analysis, RTOs and RPOs.
blocks.example: Recovery priorities list the payment switch first, then core banking, then email.

blocks.text: **Perform Automated Backups.** Perform automated backups of in-scope enterprise assets weekly or more often, depending on data sensitivity.
blocks.practice: Automated backup jobs with monitoring and alerts on failure; include SaaS data (e.g. Microsoft 365).
blocks.example: Nightly automated backups replace a manual weekly process that was often skipped.

blocks.text: **Protect Recovery Data.** Protect recovery data with controls equivalent to the original data, such as encryption or data separation.
blocks.practice: Encrypt backups, restrict backup admin access and require MFA on the backup console.
blocks.example: Backup encryption keys and admin accounts are separate from the production domain, so a domain compromise doesn't expose backups.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain an Isolated Instance of Recovery Data.** Establish and maintain an isolated instance of recovery data, for example version-controlled backups in offline, cloud or off-site systems.
blocks.practice: Immutable or air-gapped backups, separate credentials and network isolation.
blocks.example: Immutable cloud backups survive a ransomware attack that deleted every backup reachable from the domain.

blocks.text: **Test Data Recovery.** Test backup recovery quarterly or more often for a sample of in-scope assets.
blocks.practice: Scheduled restore tests measuring actual time against RTOs; document results.
blocks.example: A quarterly restore test shows the ERP takes 36 hours to restore against a 12-hour objective, triggering a redesign.

blocks.text: Establish, implement and actively manage network devices to prevent attackers from exploiting vulnerable network services and access points.
Why it matters

Routers, firewalls, VPN concentrators and switches are high-value targets: they sit at trust boundaries, are often internet-facing and are frequently left unpatched. Many major breaches in recent years started with a network edge device.

blocks.title: Executive view
blocks.text: Edge devices (VPNs, firewalls, load balancers) have been among the most exploited technologies in recent years. Keeping them supported and patched (12.1) is IG1 for a reason; budget for their replacement before end of support.
Safeguards

**Ensure Network Infrastructure is Up-to-Date.** Keep network infrastructure up to date, for example by running the latest stable software release or using supported network-as-a-service offerings. Check software versions for support monthly or more often.
blocks.practice: Track firmware versions and end-of-support dates for network devices; patch edge devices urgently.
blocks.example: A monthly firmware review flags a VPN appliance two versions behind a patch for an actively exploited flaw.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Secure Network Architecture.** Establish and maintain a secure network architecture that addresses at least segmentation, least privilege and availability.
blocks.practice: Documented network zones, trust boundaries and redundancy design.
blocks.example: The architecture separates user, server, management and OT networks with controlled conduits between them.

blocks.text: **Securely Manage Network Infrastructure.** Manage network infrastructure securely, for example with version-controlled infrastructure as code and secure protocols such as SSH and HTTPS.
blocks.practice: Config management with backups, change control, and secure management protocols only.
blocks.example: All firewall changes go through a Git repository with peer review and automated deployment.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain Architecture Diagram(s).** Establish and maintain network architecture diagrams and/or other network documentation. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Current diagrams showing zones, key devices, cloud connectivity and external connections.
blocks.example: Up-to-date diagrams let incident responders quickly see which segments a compromised server could reach.

blocks.text: **Centralize Network Authentication, Authorization, and Auditing (AAA).** Centralise authentication, authorisation and auditing for network infrastructure, so administrators log in to network devices with individual, centrally managed accounts and their actions are recorded.
blocks.practice: TACACS+ or RADIUS integrated with the directory for device administration.
blocks.example: Network admins log into switches with directory accounts through TACACS+, so every change is attributed to a person.

blocks.text: **Use of Secure Network Management and Communication Protocols.** Use secure network management and communication protocols, for example 802.1X and WPA2 Enterprise or better.
blocks.practice: WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise for corporate Wi-Fi, SNMPv3, SSH, no Telnet.
blocks.example: Moving office Wi-Fi from a shared password to WPA3-Enterprise with certificates removes the risk of leaked Wi-Fi keys.

blocks.text: **Ensure Remote Devices Utilize a VPN and are Connecting to an Enterprise's AAA Infrastructure.** Require users to authenticate to enterprise-managed VPN and authentication services before accessing enterprise resources from end-user devices.
blocks.practice: Always-on VPN or zero trust network access tied to the identity provider.
blocks.example: Remote staff reach internal apps only through ZTNA with device posture checks.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain Dedicated Computing Resources for All Administrative Work.** Establish and maintain dedicated computing resources, physically or logically separated, for all administrative work. Segment them from the primary network and don't give them internet access.
blocks.practice: Privileged access workstations (PAWs) or hardened jump hosts.
blocks.example: Domain administrators work only from privileged access workstations with no email or web access.

blocks.text: Operate processes and tooling to establish and maintain comprehensive network monitoring and defence against security threats across the enterprise's network infrastructure and user base.
Why it matters

Prevention eventually fails. Network monitoring gives you the chance to spot lateral movement, command-and-control traffic and data exfiltration before they turn into a full breach. Note that Control 13 has no IG1 Safeguards: it needs tools and skills that small teams usually source as a managed service.

blocks.title: Managed detection
blocks.text: For IG2 organisations without a 24x7 team, a managed detection and response (MDR) or managed SOC service is the practical way to meet 13.1-13.3 and 13.6.
Safeguards

**Centralize Security Event Alerting.** Centralise security event alerting across enterprise assets for correlation and analysis. Good practice is a SIEM with vendor-defined correlation alerts; a log analytics platform with security correlation alerts also qualifies.
blocks.practice: SIEM or XDR platform receiving logs from Control 8 sources, with tuned correlation rules and on-call alert routing.
blocks.example: The SIEM correlates a VPN login from abroad with a new mailbox forwarding rule and raises one high-priority alert.

blocks.text: **Deploy a Host-Based Intrusion Detection Solution.** Deploy host-based intrusion detection on enterprise assets where appropriate or supported, to spot suspicious activity on the host itself.
blocks.practice: EDR detection capability or host IDS agents on servers and endpoints.
blocks.example: Host-based detection flags a web server spawning a command shell, indicating a web shell.

blocks.text: **Deploy a Network Intrusion Detection Solution.** Deploy a network intrusion detection solution where appropriate, such as a network IDS or equivalent cloud provider service.
blocks.practice: NIDS/NDR sensors at key network points; cloud-native threat detection in cloud environments.
blocks.example: Network detection spots Kerberoasting traffic from a compromised workstation.

blocks.text: **Perform Traffic Filtering Between Network Segments.** Filter traffic between network segments where appropriate, allowing only the flows each zone actually needs.
blocks.practice: Internal firewalls or cloud security groups enforce allowed flows between zones.
blocks.example: Filtering between the user and server networks blocks a worm's SMB-based spread.

blocks.text: **Manage Access Control for Remote Assets.** Manage access control for remotely connecting assets, granting access based on up-to-date anti-malware, compliance with secure configuration and up-to-date OS and applications.
blocks.practice: Device posture checks in VPN or ZTNA (compliant device required).
blocks.example: A laptop with outdated antivirus is blocked from connecting to internal apps until it is remediated.

blocks.text: **Collect Network Traffic Flow Logs.** Collect network traffic flow logs and/or network traffic from network devices to review and alert on.
blocks.practice: NetFlow/IPFIX, cloud VPC flow logs, sent to analytics.
blocks.example: VPC flow logs reveal a database server sending 40 GB to an unknown IP address overnight.

blocks.text: **Deploy a Host-Based Intrusion Prevention Solution.** Deploy a host-based intrusion prevention solution where appropriate or supported, such as an EDR client or host-based IPS agent.
blocks.practice: EDR in block mode, with automatic isolation for high-confidence detections.
blocks.example: EDR automatically isolates a host after detecting ransomware behaviour.

blocks.text: **Deploy a Network Intrusion Prevention Solution.** Deploy a network intrusion prevention solution where appropriate, such as a network IPS or equivalent cloud provider service.
blocks.practice: IPS on next-generation firewalls, tuned to avoid blocking legitimate traffic.
blocks.example: The perimeter IPS blocks exploitation attempts against an unpatched web server while the patch is scheduled.

blocks.text: **Deploy Port-Level Access Control.** Deploy port-level access control using 802.1X or similar network access control, possibly with certificates and user and/or device authentication.
blocks.practice: NAC with 802.1X on wired and wireless networks; guest and unknown devices placed on isolated VLANs.
blocks.example: An unauthorised device plugged into an office wall port is placed on a quarantine VLAN automatically.

blocks.text: **Perform Application Layer Filtering.** Perform application layer filtering, for example with a filtering proxy, application layer firewall or gateway.
blocks.practice: Web application firewalls, secure web gateways, API gateways.
blocks.example: A WAF blocks SQL injection attempts against a legacy customer portal.

blocks.text: **Tune Security Event Alerting Thresholds.** Review and tune the thresholds that trigger security alerts monthly or more often, to cut noise and close detection gaps.
blocks.practice: Review false positives and missed detections; adjust rules; track alert quality metrics.
blocks.example: Monthly tuning cuts false positives by 40%, letting analysts spend time on real threats.

quiz.q: How often should backup recovery be tested under 11.5?
quiz.explain: Quarterly or more often, for a sample of in-scope assets.

quiz.q: An isolated instance of recovery data (11.4) is in which IG?
quiz.explain: 11.4 is IG1, reflecting how often attackers target backups.

quiz.q: How often should automated backups run at minimum under 11.2?
quiz.explain: Weekly or more often, based on data sensitivity.

quiz.q: Privileged access workstations for administrative work map to...
quiz.explain: 12.8 Establish and Maintain Dedicated Computing Resources for All Administrative Work (IG3).

quiz.q: How many IG1 Safeguards does Control 13 have?
quiz.explain: None. Control 13 starts at IG2.

quiz.q: Port-level access control using 802.1X is...
quiz.explain: 13.9 Deploy Port-Level Access Control (IG3).

chapters.title: Controls 14-16: People, providers and code
chapters.summary: Security awareness, service providers and application software security: 30 Safeguards.

sections.title: Control 14: Security Awareness and Skills Training

blocks.text: Establish and maintain a security awareness programme to influence behaviour among the workforce so they are security-conscious and properly skilled to reduce cybersecurity risk.
Why it matters

People are targeted because they are easier to trick than systems are to break. Eight of the nine Safeguards are IG1: awareness is cheap, and a workforce that reports phishing quickly shortens every attack.

blocks.title: Measure behaviour, not completion
blocks.text: Completion rates prove people clicked through a course. Phishing report rates, time-to-report and repeat-clicker trends show whether behaviour changed.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness Program.** Establish and maintain a security awareness programme that teaches the workforce to use enterprise assets and data securely. Train at hire and at least annually; review content annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Documented programme with annual plan, audience, topics and metrics.
blocks.example: The awareness plan combines onboarding training, a yearly refresher, monthly phishing simulations and short topical videos.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce Members to Recognize Social Engineering Attacks.** Train the workforce to recognise social engineering attacks such as phishing, pretexting and tailgating.
blocks.practice: Scenario-based training and phishing simulations with immediate feedback.
blocks.example: Finance staff learn to verify bank-detail change requests by calling a known number, which stops a business email compromise attempt.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce Members on Authentication Best Practices.** Train the workforce on authentication best practices, such as MFA, password composition and credential management.
blocks.practice: Cover password managers, MFA fatigue attacks and never sharing codes.
blocks.example: An employee rejects an unexpected MFA push and reports it, revealing that their password had been stolen.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce on Data Handling Best Practices.** Train the workforce to identify, store, transfer, archive and destroy sensitive data properly, including clear screen and clear desk habits.
blocks.practice: Tie training to the classification scheme (3.7) and handling rules.
blocks.example: Staff learn to lock screens and wipe whiteboards after meetings in shared spaces.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce Members on Causes of Unintentional Data Exposure.** Train the workforce on causes of unintentional data exposure, such as mis-delivered data, lost devices or publishing to unintended audiences.
blocks.practice: Examples of autocomplete errors in email, public sharing links and lost laptops.
blocks.example: After training, a user notices that a shared link is set to "anyone with the link" and restricts it.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce Members on Recognizing and Reporting Security Incidents.** Train the workforce to recognise a potential incident and report it.
blocks.practice: Make reporting easy (a report button, one clear contact) and thank people for reporting.
blocks.example: Five staff report the same phishing email within minutes, letting the team purge it from all mailboxes.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce on How to Identify and Report if Their Enterprise Assets are Missing Security Updates.** Train the workforce to verify and report out-of-date software patches or failures in automated processes and tools, notifying IT of failures.
blocks.practice: Show staff how to check update status and where to report problems.
blocks.example: A user reports that their laptop hasn't updated in two months, uncovering a broken patch deployment ring.

blocks.text: **Train Workforce on the Dangers of Connecting to and Transmitting Enterprise Data Over Insecure Networks.** Train the workforce on the dangers of connecting to and transmitting enterprise data over insecure networks. Remote workers should learn to configure home networks securely.
blocks.practice: Cover public Wi-Fi, VPN use and home router security basics.
blocks.example: Remote staff receive a short guide to changing default router passwords and updating router firmware.

blocks.text: **Conduct Role-Specific Security Awareness and Skills Training.** Conduct role-specific security awareness and skills training, such as secure administration for IT staff, OWASP Top 10 for developers and advanced social engineering training for high-profile roles.
blocks.practice: Identify high-risk roles and give them targeted training.
blocks.example: Executives and their assistants receive training on whaling and deepfake voice fraud.

blocks.text: Develop a process to evaluate service providers that hold sensitive data or are responsible for critical IT platforms or processes, to make sure they protect those platforms and data appropriately.
Why it matters
Outsourcing a service does not outsource the risk. Many major breaches came through a supplier: a managed service provider, a software update or a SaaS platform.

blocks.title: Link to NIST CSF
blocks.text: Control 15 lines up closely with the CSF 2.0 GV.SC category (Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management). If you already run a CSF-aligned third-party risk programme, map it rather than building a second one.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Providers.** Maintain an inventory of all known service providers with their classification and an enterprise contact for each. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Supplier register from procurement and finance, enriched with data access and criticality.
blocks.example: Building the register from accounts payable reveals 70 SaaS tools bought on corporate cards.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Service Provider Management Policy.** Establish and maintain a service provider management policy covering classification, inventory, assessment, monitoring and decommissioning. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Third-party risk policy owned jointly by procurement, legal and security.
blocks.example: The policy defines how suppliers are tiered and what assurance each tier must provide.

blocks.text: **Classify Service Providers.** Classify service providers using characteristics such as data sensitivity, data volume, availability requirements, applicable regulations, inherent risk and mitigated risk. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Tiering questionnaire at onboarding; critical, high, medium, low.
blocks.example: The cloud hosting provider and payroll processor are classified critical; the office catering company is low.

blocks.text: **Ensure Service Provider Contracts Include Security Requirements.** Make sure service provider contracts include security requirements such as minimum programme requirements, incident and breach notification, encryption and data disposal. Review contracts annually.
blocks.practice: Standard security schedule and data processing agreement templates.
blocks.example: New contracts require breach notification within 24 hours and certified data deletion at contract end.

blocks.text: **Assess Service Providers.** Assess service providers in line with the policy, using standardised reports such as SOC 2 or PCI AoC, questionnaires or other rigorous methods. Reassess at least annually or when contracts change.
blocks.practice: Assessment depth scaled by tier; track findings and follow-ups.
blocks.example: A critical supplier's SOC 2 report shows an exception in access reviews; remediation is tracked as a contract condition.

blocks.text: **Monitor Service Providers.** Monitor service providers in line with the policy, for example through periodic reassessment, reviewing release notes and dark web monitoring.
blocks.practice: Security ratings services, news monitoring, and contractual reporting.
blocks.example: Monitoring spots a supplier's credentials in a dark web dump, and the enterprise rotates the shared API keys.

blocks.text: **Securely Decommission Service Providers.** Decommission service providers securely: deactivate user and service accounts, end data flows and securely dispose of enterprise data in their systems.
blocks.practice: Exit checklist triggered by contract termination.
blocks.example: When switching CRM vendors, the company revokes all API tokens and obtains a data destruction certificate.

blocks.text: Manage the security life cycle of in-house developed, hosted or acquired software to prevent, detect and remediate security weaknesses before they can affect the enterprise.
Why it matters

Applications, especially web apps and APIs, are exposed directly to the internet and handle sensitive data. Control 16 has no IG1 Safeguards because it applies to organisations that develop or heavily customise software.

blocks.title: Related frameworks
blocks.text: Control 16 aligns with the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218), OWASP SAMM and the OWASP Top 10. Use them for depth; use the CIS Safeguards as the checklist of what must exist.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Secure Application Development Process.** Establish and maintain a secure application development process covering secure design standards, secure coding, developer training, vulnerability management, third-party code security and security testing. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: A documented secure SDLC with security gates in the CI/CD pipeline.
blocks.example: The SDLC requires threat modelling for new features, SAST on every pull request and a security sign-off before major releases.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Process to Accept and Address Software Vulnerabilities.** Establish and maintain a process to accept and address reports of software vulnerabilities, including a way for outsiders to report. Include a vulnerability handling policy, owners, intake, assignment, remediation and retesting, using a tracking system.
blocks.practice: Vulnerability disclosure policy, security.txt, PSIRT process.
blocks.example: A researcher reports an API flaw through the disclosure page; it is triaged in 2 days and fixed in 10.

blocks.text: **Perform Root Cause Analysis on Security Vulnerabilities.** Perform root cause analysis on security vulnerabilities so development teams fix underlying issues, not just individual bugs.
blocks.practice: Post-fix reviews asking why the flaw was introduced and how to prevent the class of bug.
blocks.example: Root cause analysis of repeated injection bugs leads to adopting a parameterised query library everywhere.

blocks.text: **Establish and Manage an Inventory of Third-Party Software Components.** Establish and manage an up-to-date inventory of third-party components used in development (a bill of materials), including planned components and their risks. Evaluate monthly for changes and support status.
blocks.practice: Software composition analysis generating SBOMs per application.
blocks.example: When a critical library vulnerability is announced, the SBOM shows within an hour which 14 applications are affected.

blocks.text: **Use Up-to-Date and Trusted Third-Party Software Components.** Use up-to-date, trusted third-party components: established frameworks and libraries from trusted sources, or evaluated for vulnerabilities before use.
blocks.practice: Approved package registries, dependency pinning, automated update PRs.
blocks.example: The build pipeline pulls packages only from an internal mirror that blocks known-malicious packages.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain a Severity Rating System and Process for Application Vulnerabilities.** Establish and maintain a severity rating system and process for application vulnerabilities to prioritise fixes, including a minimum security bar for releasing code.
blocks.practice: Severity matrix (e.g. CVSS-based plus business context) with release-blocking thresholds.
blocks.example: No release can ship with open critical or high findings unless the CISO approves an exception.

blocks.text: **Use Standard Hardening Configuration Templates for Application Infrastructure.** Use standard, industry-recommended hardening templates for application infrastructure (servers, databases, web servers, containers, PaaS and SaaS), and don't let in-house software weaken hardening.
blocks.practice: CIS Benchmarks for the web server, database and container platform; hardened base images.
blocks.example: All containers build from a hardened base image checked against the CIS Docker Benchmark.

blocks.text: **Separate Production and Non-Production Systems.** Keep production and non-production (development, test, staging) environments separate.
blocks.practice: Separate accounts, networks and credentials; no production data in test without masking.
blocks.example: Test environments use masked data, so a breach of the test system exposes no real customer information.

blocks.text: **Train Developers in Application Security Concepts and Secure Coding.** Train all software development staff in writing secure code for their environment, at least annually, building a security culture in the team.
blocks.practice: Language-specific secure coding training and security champions in each team.
blocks.example: Each squad has a security champion who attends monthly sessions and reviews risky changes.

blocks.text: **Apply Secure Design Principles in Application Architectures.** Apply secure design principles in application architecture, such as least privilege, complete mediation and never trusting user input, with explicit input validation and a minimal attack surface.
blocks.practice: Architecture review checklists; input validation and output encoding standards.
blocks.example: The design review requires every API to validate input size, type and format before processing.

blocks.text: **Leverage Vetted Modules or Services for Application Security Components.** Use vetted modules or services for security components such as identity management, encryption and logging, rather than building your own.
blocks.practice: Use platform identity services and standard crypto libraries; never roll your own crypto.
blocks.example: The team replaces a home-grown password hashing routine with the framework's vetted implementation.

blocks.text: **Implement Code-Level Security Checks.** Apply static and dynamic analysis tools during the application lifecycle to check that secure coding practices are followed.
blocks.practice: SAST in pull requests, DAST in staging, secrets scanning.
blocks.example: Secrets scanning blocks a commit containing a cloud access key.

blocks.text: **Conduct Application Penetration Testing.** Conduct application penetration testing. For critical applications, authenticated testing is better at finding business logic flaws than automated scanning.
blocks.practice: Annual and pre-release tests by skilled testers, both authenticated and unauthenticated.
blocks.example: An authenticated pen test finds that customers can view each other's statements by changing an ID in the URL.

blocks.text: **Conduct Threat Modeling.** Conduct threat modelling to identify and address design flaws before code is written, using trained people to assess each entry point and access level.
blocks.practice: STRIDE or similar methods applied to new systems and major changes.
blocks.example: Threat modelling a new mobile banking feature identifies a missing rate limit on OTP verification before development starts.

quiz.q: How many of Control 14's nine Safeguards are IG1?
quiz.explain: 14.1-14.8 are IG1; role-specific training (14.9) is IG2.

quiz.q: Which Control 15 Safeguard is IG1?
quiz.explain: Only 15.1 is IG1.

quiz.q: A software bill of materials maps to...
quiz.explain: 16.4 Establish and Manage an Inventory of Third-Party Software Components.

quiz.q: Threat modelling (16.14) is in which IG?
Which type of report does 15.5 mention for assessing providers?
options: SOC 2 and PCI Attestation of Compliance
quiz.explain: Standardised reports such as SOC 2 and PCI AoC, questionnaires or other rigorous processes.

quiz.q: Control 16 applies from which IG?
quiz.explain: Control 16 has no IG1 Safeguards; it starts at IG2.

chapters.title: Controls 17-18: Respond and test
chapters.summary: Incident response management and penetration testing: 14 Safeguards.

blocks.text: Establish a programme to develop and maintain an incident response capability (policies, plans, procedures, defined roles, training and communications) to prepare for, detect and quickly respond to an attack.
Why it matters

Every organisation will have incidents. The difference between a contained event and a crisis is usually preparation: knowing who is in charge, who to call and how to communicate when email itself may be compromised.

blocks.title: Executive view
blocks.text: Run at least one tabletop exercise a year with the executive team (17.7). Decisions about ransom payment, regulator notification and public statements are far better rehearsed than improvised.
Safeguards

**Designate Personnel to Manage Incident Handling.** Designate one key person, and at least one backup, to manage the incident handling process. They coordinate and document response and recovery and may be internal, third-party or both; if a third party is used, an internal person oversees its work.
blocks.practice: Named incident manager and deputy in the IR plan; retainer with an IR firm if needed.
blocks.example: A mid-size insurer names its IT manager as incident lead, a deputy, and an external IR retainer for major incidents.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain Contact Information for Reporting Security Incidents.** Maintain contact information for parties who must be informed of incidents: internal staff, vendors, law enforcement, cyber insurers, government agencies, ISACs and others. Verify contacts annually.
blocks.practice: Contact list stored offline as well as online, since systems may be unavailable.
blocks.example: When email is down during a ransomware attack, the printed contact list lets the team reach the insurer and CERT.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain an Enterprise Process for Reporting Incidents.** Establish and maintain a process for the workforce to report security incidents, including timeframe, who to report to, how, and the minimum information needed. Make it available to all staff; review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Simple reporting channels (report button, hotline, service desk category) publicised to all staff.
blocks.example: The intranet homepage shows a single "Report a security concern" link and phone number.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain an Incident Response Process.** Establish and maintain an incident response process covering roles and responsibilities, compliance requirements and a communication plan. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: IR plan and playbooks (ransomware, BEC, data breach) aligned to NIST SP 800-61.
blocks.example: The ransomware playbook defines isolation steps, decision authority on shutdown and regulator notification timelines.

blocks.text: **Assign Key Roles and Responsibilities.** Assign key incident response roles and responsibilities across legal, IT, security, facilities, PR, HR, responders and analysts as applicable. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: RACI for incident roles, with deputies.
blocks.example: Legal owns breach notification decisions; PR owns public statements; the CISO leads technical response.

blocks.text: **Define Mechanisms for Communicating During Incident Response.** Decide which primary and secondary mechanisms (phone, email, letters and so on) will be used to communicate during an incident, remembering that some channels, like email, may be affected. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Out-of-band channels such as a separate messaging workspace or phone bridge.
blocks.example: The crisis team switches to a pre-arranged out-of-band chat because attackers may be reading corporate email.

blocks.text: **Conduct Routine Incident Response Exercises.** Plan and run routine incident response exercises and scenarios for key personnel, testing communications, decision-making and workflows, at least annually.
blocks.practice: Tabletop exercises, technical simulations and executive crisis exercises.
blocks.example: A tabletop exercise reveals nobody knew who could authorise shutting down the e-commerce site.

blocks.text: **Conduct Post-Incident Reviews.** Conduct post-incident reviews to identify lessons learned and follow-up actions that prevent recurrence.
blocks.practice: Blameless reviews with tracked actions.
blocks.example: A post-incident review leads to enforcing MFA on the VPN that the attacker had used.

blocks.text: **Establish and Maintain Security Incident Thresholds.** Establish and maintain security incident thresholds, at a minimum distinguishing an event from an incident, with examples such as abnormal activity, vulnerabilities, weaknesses, data breaches and privacy incidents. Review annually or after significant change.
blocks.practice: Severity matrix and incident criteria in the IR plan.
blocks.example: Criteria define that any confirmed access to personal data is a major incident requiring legal involvement.

blocks.text: Test the effectiveness and resilience of enterprise assets by identifying and exploiting weaknesses in controls (people, processes and technology) and simulating the objectives and actions of an attacker.
Why it matters
Penetration testing validates whether the other 17 Controls actually work together. It is placed last, and has no IG1 Safeguards, because testing is most valuable once basic hygiene is in place.

blocks.title: Pen test is not vulnerability scanning
blocks.text: A vulnerability scan lists potential weaknesses automatically. A penetration test uses skilled people to chain weaknesses and prove impact. You need both; they answer different questions.
Safeguards

**Establish and Maintain a Penetration Testing Program.** Establish and maintain a penetration testing programme suited to the enterprise's size, complexity and maturity, covering scope (network, web apps, APIs, hosted services, physical), frequency, limitations, contacts, remediation and retesting.
blocks.practice: Programme document defining test types, frequency, rules of engagement and remediation tracking.
blocks.example: The programme requires annual external and internal tests, plus tests before launching any new internet-facing system.

blocks.text: **Perform Periodic External Penetration Tests.** Perform external penetration tests at least annually, including reconnaissance for exploitable information, by a qualified party. Tests can be clear box or opaque box.
blocks.practice: Qualified testers (e.g. CREST, OSCP-certified) with clear rules of engagement.
blocks.example: An external test finds an exposed admin panel via reconnaissance of old DNS records.

blocks.text: **Remediate Penetration Test Findings.** Remediate penetration test findings according to the enterprise's remediation scope and prioritisation policy.
blocks.practice: Track findings in the same system as vulnerabilities with SLAs; retest critical fixes.
blocks.example: All critical findings are fixed within 30 days and verified by a retest.

blocks.text: **Validate Security Measures.** Validate security measures after each penetration test and, if needed, adjust rulesets and capabilities to detect the techniques used.
blocks.practice: Purple teaming: check whether the SOC saw each test step and tune detections.
blocks.example: The SOC missed the testers' lateral movement, so new detection rules are written and tested.

blocks.text: **Perform Periodic Internal Penetration Tests.** Perform internal penetration tests at least annually. Tests can be clear box or opaque box.
blocks.practice: Assume-breach tests starting from a standard user workstation.
blocks.example: An internal test goes from a standard user to domain admin in four hours through a misconfigured certificate template.

quiz.q: Safeguard 17.1 requires...
options: One key person and at least one backup to manage incident handling
quiz.explain: Designate a key person and a backup; if a third party is used, an internal person oversees it.

quiz.q: Which incident response Safeguards are IG1?
quiz.explain: Personnel, contacts, and the workforce reporting process.

quiz.q: How often should incident response exercises run under 17.7?
quiz.explain: At least annually.

quiz.q: External penetration tests (18.2) must happen at least...
quiz.explain: No less than annually, by a qualified party.

quiz.q: Adjusting detection rules after a pen test maps to...
quiz.explain: 18.4 Validate Security Measures (IG3).

chapters.title: CIS Benchmarks: the essentials
chapters.summary: What Benchmarks are, what they cover, how they're made, profiles and formats.

blocks.text: A **CIS Benchmark** is a best-practice guide for the secure configuration of a specific technology: an operating system, cloud account, database, network device, browser or application. CIS describes them as the only consensus-based security configuration guides developed and accepted by government, business, industry and academia.

CIS publishes **more than 100 Benchmarks across 25+ vendor product families**. Each Benchmark targets a specific product and version, for example Microsoft Windows 11 Enterprise, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, Amazon Web Services Foundations or Microsoft 365 Foundations.

rows: What to do and in what order
Recommendation (e.g. "Ensure SSH root login is disabled")
Dozens to several hundred recommendations per Benchmark

blocks.title: Where Benchmarks fit
blocks.text: Benchmarks are the "how" for Control 4 (secure configuration) and support many others: 5 (accounts), 6 (MFA), 8 (logging), 9 (browsers), 10 (malware defences), 12 (network devices) and 16.7 (hardening application infrastructure).

headers: Examples (check the CIS site for current versions)
rows: Microsoft Windows 10/11 Enterprise, Windows Server, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Ubuntu Linux, Debian, Oracle Linux, Apple macOS, IBM AIX

Amazon Web Services Foundations, Microsoft Azure Foundations, Google Cloud Platform Foundation, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Foundations, plus service-specific ones such as compute or database services
Microsoft 365 Foundations, Google Workspace Foundations, Microsoft Office, Microsoft Intune
Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Apache HTTP Server, Apache Tomcat, NGINX, Microsoft IIS
Docker, Kubernetes, and managed Kubernetes such as Amazon EKS, Azure AKS and Google GKE
Cisco IOS and ASA, Palo Alto Networks firewalls, Fortinet FortiGate, Juniper, Check Point
Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge
Apple iOS and iPadOS, Google Android
Software supply chain security guidance and CI/CD platforms

blocks.text: Benchmarks are written through a **consensus process** run on **CIS WorkBench**, a free community platform:

items: **Scope:** CIS and the community decide the target product and version.
**Draft:** volunteer subject-matter experts, vendors and CIS staff write recommendations.
**Consensus:** recommendations are discussed and debated in WorkBench threads until the community agrees.
**Publish:** the Benchmark is released with a version number (e.g. v3.0.0) and a change history.
**Maintain:** new product versions and community feedback lead to updates. CIS aims to update Windows Benchmarks within 90 days of a new Windows release.

blocks.title: You can contribute
blocks.text: Anyone can register on CIS WorkBench to comment on drafts, report issues and follow updates for the Benchmarks they use. It is also where older Benchmark versions are archived.
Every recommendation belongs to one or more **profiles**, which let you choose how far to go:

rows: Base recommendations that can be implemented fairly promptly, reduce the attack surface and are designed not to have an extensive performance impact or break functionality
Defense in depth for environments where security is paramount; includes all of Level 1 plus additional recommendations

chapters.title: CIS tools and membership
chapters.summary: CIS-CAT, Hardened Images, Build Kits, WorkBench, SecureSuite and the ISACs.

blocks.text: The **CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT)** scans systems against CIS Benchmarks and reports a compliance score.

rows: All supported Benchmarks, including tailored versions built in WorkBench
Views results across the estate and over time; manages exceptions
Multiple report formats; results mapped to CIS Controls and Implementation Groups

blocks.title: Try it first
blocks.text: CIS-CAT Lite is a quick way to see how far a Windows or macOS laptop is from Level 1. It is a learning and spot-check tool; use Pro or a certified scanner for enterprise-wide assessment.

**CIS Hardened Images** are virtual machine images pre-configured to a CIS Benchmark, available through the AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud marketplaces on a pay-per-use basis. Most are hardened to Level 1; some Level 2 and STIG options exist.

items: **Benefit:** start secure instead of hardening after deployment.
**Cloud exceptions:** a few recommendations are not applied because they would break cloud functionality (for example remote access needs). CIS documents these.
**Still your responsibility:** patching, application configuration, identity, and anything you install on top.
**Validate:** scan with CIS-CAT to confirm compliance after your own changes.

blocks.text: **CIS Build Kits** apply Benchmark settings in bulk: Group Policy objects for Windows and scripts for Linux. They are available to SecureSuite members and save weeks of manual work.

blocks.title: Build Kits are not a shortcut past testing
blocks.text: Applying a full Level 1 GPO to production without piloting it is a common cause of outages (broken legacy authentication, blocked remote administration). Import it, review settings against your deviations, pilot, then roll out in rings.

WorkBench is the free community platform where Benchmarks are developed and maintained. Registered users can download Benchmarks, join discussions, report issues, follow milestones and access older versions. SecureSuite members can also create **tailored Benchmarks** (for example your approved deviations built in) that CIS-CAT Pro can then assess against.

**CIS SecureSuite** is CIS's paid membership. It bundles CIS-CAT Pro, Build Kits, additional Benchmark formats, remediation content, CSAT Pro and member support. There are memberships for organisations securing their own systems and for vendors and service providers who embed CIS content or certify products. Check the CIS website for current categories and pricing.

blocks.title: Is it worth it?
blocks.text: For organisations hardening hundreds of servers or multiple platforms, the Build Kits and CIS-CAT Pro typically save more engineering time than the membership costs. For a small organisation, free PDFs, CIS-CAT Lite and native tools may be enough.

CIS hosts the **Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC)** for US state, local, tribal and territorial governments, and the **Elections Infrastructure ISAC (EI-ISAC)**. They share threat intelligence, advisories and incident support.
Federal funding for MS-ISAC through its CISA cooperative agreement ended in September 2025, and MS-ISAC moved to a paid membership model.

blocks.title: Outside the US
blocks.text: The ISACs are US-focused. Organisations elsewhere get similar value from their national CERT or CSIRT, sector ISACs such as FS-ISAC for financial services, and regional sharing groups.

chapters.title: Assessing and managing a CIS programme
chapters.summary: CSAT, the Assessment Specification, CIS RAM, mappings, companion guides and metrics.

blocks.text: **CSAT** helps an organisation track implementation of the CIS Safeguards over time. A hosted version is available free, and **CSAT Pro** (for SecureSuite members) can be run on your own infrastructure.
CSAT rates each Safeguard on four questions:

items: Is there a **policy** defined?
Is the Safeguard **implemented**?
Is it **automated or technically enforced**?
Is it **reported to the business**?

blocks.title: Why four questions
blocks.text: The split shows where the gap really is. Many organisations have a policy and partial implementation but nothing automated or reported, which is why controls drift.

The Assessment Specification describes, for each Safeguard, how to measure it: **dependencies** (other Safeguards it relies on), **inputs** (e.g. the asset inventory), **operations** (steps to assess), **measures** (counts) and **metrics** (ratios).

blocks.title: Example: Safeguard 3.6
blocks.text: Inputs: the asset inventory and authorised software inventory. Measures: number of end-user devices (M1), number with encryption software installed (M2), number properly configured. Metric: encryption coverage = M2 / M1. That ratio is a ready-made KPI for your dashboard.
Use it as an audit script: it turns "encrypt end-user devices" into a measurable test with clear evidence.

**CIS RAM** (version 2.1 for Controls v8) is a method for deciding which Safeguards to implement, and how far, based on risk. It builds on the **Duty of Care Risk Analysis (DoCRA)** standard: a safeguard is reasonable if its burden is not greater than the risk it reduces, considering harm to the organisation **and to others** (customers, the public).

items: Separate workbooks and guides exist for IG1, IG2 and IG3.
You define impact and likelihood criteria and an acceptable risk level tied to your mission and obligations.
For each Safeguard you assess current risk, proposed treatment, and the burden of that treatment.
The result is a defensible, documented rationale, useful when regulators or courts ask whether security was "reasonable".

blocks.title: Why lawyers like it
blocks.text: DoCRA-based analysis frames security decisions the way regulators and courts often judge them: did the organisation weigh the harm to others against the cost of prevention? CIS RAM produces that record.

CIS publishes mappings from the Safeguards to many frameworks, browsable in the **CIS Controls Navigator**: NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, PCI DSS v4, SOC 2 and others. An indicative view:
